catalog_quote: Le bakwé est une langue musicale, c’est-à-dire que les mots ne se distinguent pas seulement par les lettres, mais aussi par leur mélodie. La hauteur musicale avec laquelle on prononce les mots est appelée le ton du mot. En bakwé, il y a trois niveaux de tons, qu’on appelle haut, moyen et bas. Le ton haut est marqué par une apostrophe au début du mot. ... Le ton moyen se pronoce à une hauteur moyenne. N’étant ni haut ni bas, il nˈest pas marqué par un signe tonal. ... Le ton bas est marqué par un tiret au début du mot. ... Jusqu’à maintenant nous avons seulement vu des exemples de mots ayant une seule syllabe. Si le mot est plus long, il consiste en deux, trois, quatre et même plus de syllabes, dont chacune porte au moins un ton. Cependant, il suffit de marquer le ton de la première syllabe du mot pour quˈun locuteur bakwé puisse lire le mot correctement. [p. 24:] Dans ce schème, la voix descend au cours du mot. On distingue deux schèmes descendants en bakwé: haut-moyen et haut-bas. Le schème haut-bas est cependant très rare.

new_statements.translation: Bakwé is a musical language, that is, words are distinguished not only by their letters but also by their melody. The musical pitch with which words are pronounced is called the tone of the word. In Bakwé there are three tone levels, called high, mid and low. [...] If the word is longer, it consists of two, three, four or even more syllables, each of which carries at least one tone. However, it suffices to mark the tone of the first syllable of the word for a Bakwé speaker to read the word correctly.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bakwé is a register-tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low) plus contour tones written with doubled/tripled vowels; every syllable bears a tone and nouns have lexical tone melodies (level H, level M, rising L-M, L-H, M-H, L-H-M). No source opened says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be stated; the three-level analysis is independently confirmed by Vogler 2017, p. 33 ('Le bakwé est une langue à trois niveaux de registres').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone notes: proper names may be written without tone marks; a word-final high tone 'belongs to the preceding vowel' (Syllabaire 2019, p. 9; Guide de prononciation).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word (lexical tone of nouns and verbs, citation forms in a literacy primer); the tone-melody classes are given for simple nouns. The primer is a literacy/orthography guide by the Bakwé translation-literacy project (SIL-facilitated), not a linguistic phonology; it describes the dɛplɛɛ (Deple) dialect used for the orthography (dictionary and syllabaire are explicitly 'en dɛplɛɛ').
new_statements.identity_note: The C.T.A.B. materials describe the dɛplɛɛ (Deple) dialect of Bakwé (the dictionary and the 2019 syllabaire are explicitly 'en dɛplɛɛ'; a separate Cours-éclair exists for Nyragbi/Nigagba), spoken around Touadji II / Meagui; Ethnologue lists dialects Defa, Deple, Dafa, Nigagba, Nyinagbi, all under bakw1243 (no separate glottocodes).

[...] ‒a 1 [B] pron. [...] Notes (Grammar) Semble avoir un ton floatant, p.e. ‒a ma (B)+(M) --> ‒ama (BB).

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog record (tonal, three levels haut/moyen/bas from the 1998 Cours-éclair): the dictionary marks H/M/B tone per syllable on every entry and gives no stress statement. The printed 2006 edition's introduction (if any) remains unread.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every headword carries a lexical tone pattern in brackets ([H], [M], [B], [BM], [MH], [BHMH].. = haut/moyen/bas per syllable; 1,265 tone labels in the 1,474 captured entries) and grammar notes describe floating low tones; the captured lexicon says nothing about word stress or accent placement (the one occurrence of 'stressed' refers to an emphatic subject pronoun in a syntactic note, not word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary (print 2006 and web export 2008) describes the Dɛplɛɛ (Deple) dialect of Bakwé, the same variety as the Cours-éclair (Dèplè) behind the catalog record; Marchese 1986 is a family-wide Kru study, not a description of Bakwé.

new_statements.quote: Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones, which in this study will usually be marked in the following way: in a four-tone system, high tone will be marked by ´, mid-high tone by ', mid tone by ¯, and low tone by `. In three-tone systems, the symbol ´ will mark high, - mid, and ` low. In both three-tone and four-tone languages, mid tone is often unmarked. [...] Tone plays an extremely important role in the grammatical systems of the Kru family, making such distinctions as perfective/imperfective aspect, possessive/relative/subject pronouns, definite/indefinite, and sometimes singular/plural.
new_statements.citation: Marchese, Lynell. 1986. Tense/aspect and the development of auxiliaries in Kru languages. Dallas: SIL (Publications in Linguistics 78). xii+301 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Family-level statement: Kru languages (Bakwé included in the data base and discussed pp. 7, 9, 14, 42) have lexical and grammatical tone with three or four register tones; the phonological overview says nothing about word stress or accent and the index has no such entry. Consistent with the catalog record (Bakwé tonal, three levels per the 1998 Cours-éclair); it does not give a Bakwé-specific tone count.
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Kru languages, Bakwé among them, are register-tone languages with three or four level tones (contours analysed as sequences) carrying lexical and heavy grammatical load; the book's phonological overview treats syllable structure, segments, vowel harmony and tone only and makes no statement about word stress or accent anywhere (no index entry, no scanned hit in the pages read).
